bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 7: Computing scores in a complete search system
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, April 1, 2009 draft)

question: How can cosine scoring be computed fast enough for a real search engine, and how do scoring, proximity, indexes and query operators fit into a complete system?
contributions: Heuristics for inexact top-K retrieval (index elimination, champion lists, static quality ordering, impact ordering, cluster pruning)
Tiered indexes, proximity weighting, query parsing and aggregate scoring
Architecture of a complete search system (Fig 7.5)
How vector space scoring interacts with Boolean, wildcard and phrase operators

results.claim: Heap selection of the top K from J scored documents costs 2J comparisons to build and log J per document read off.
results.setup: Top-K selection over the J documents with non-zero cosine score; asymptotic count, no measured data.
results.quote: constructing such a heap can be performed in 2J comparison steps, following which each of the K highest scoring documents can be “read off” the heap with log J comparison steps.

results.claim: Cluster pruning picks sqrt(N) random leaders, so each leader is expected to have about sqrt(N) followers.
results.setup: Basic cluster pruning, b1 = b2 = 1; N documents in the collection.
results.quote: the expected number of followers for each leader is ≈N/

results.claim: Cluster pruning variants attach each follower to its b1 closest leaders and consider the b2 leaders closest to the query; the basic scheme is b1 = b2 = 1.
results.setup: Cluster pruning variants; raising b1 or b2 raises the chance of finding the true top K at more compute cost.
results.quote: the basic scheme above corresponds to the case b1 = b2 = 1

results.claim: Tiered indexes example uses tf thresholds of 20 for tier 1 and 10 for tier 2, with fall-back when a tier returns fewer than K results.
results.setup: Illustration on the terms and documents of Figure 6.9 (Fig 7.4); postings within a tier ordered by document ID.

results.claim: The smallest-window proximity width omega for the query 'strained mercy' in 'The quality of mercy is not strained' is 4 words.
results.setup: Proximity weighting feature omega = width in words of the smallest window containing all query terms; set to an enormous number if a term is missing.
results.quote: the smallest window for the query strained mercy would be 4.

results.setup: Net-score(q,d) = g(d) + cosine; other weightings possible and heuristic effectiveness depends on the weighting.

limits: No experiments or measured speed/quality numbers; every heuristic is described qualitatively and the authors say parameters (r, m, thresholds, b1, b2) must be tuned per collection (p.137).
Most heuristics suit free-text queries but not Boolean or phrase queries (p.137, 7.4 refs).

Dated 2008-09: scoring is TF-IDF cosine and machine-learned ranking is only sketched; no dense or learned-sparse retrieval, approximate nearest neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF), BM25 (appears elsewhere in the book, not here), WAND or block-max pruning, or neural rerankers.
The claim that web engines use 'soft conjunctive' semantics is hedged ('evidently use'), not shown.
Cluster pruning with random leaders is the book's only vector-space ANN idea; it is the ancestor of IVF-style partitioning but is not named so.
practices: Rank by relative score: set all query weights to 1 and skip query normalisation (p.135-136).
Use a heap for top K instead of sorting all J scored documents (p.136).
Drop low-idf query terms as stop words during traversal, and require many or all terms to be present, accepting that fewer than K candidates may result (p.137-138).
Precompute champion lists of r top documents per term, with r large relative to K and possibly larger for rarer terms (p.138).
Fall back through tiered indexes when a tier yields fewer than K results (p.143-144).
Add the proximity window width omega as a learned feature rather than hand-coding it (p.145).
Use a query parser that cascades from phrase to sub-phrase to bag-of-terms queries, and an aggregate scoring function to accumulate evidence (p.145-146).
Use hand-tuned scoring in stable enterprise collections and machine-learned scoring for web-scale setups with many factors (p.146).
Keep a document cache for result snippets and run spelling correction only when the original query returns too few results (p.146-147).

terms.definition: for each term t in the dictionary, the set of the r documents with the highest weights for t; the value of r is chosen in advance
a measure of quality g(d) for each document d that is query-independent and thus static, a number between zero and one
computing the score for each document as encountered during concurrent traversal of postings lists with a common ordering
scores accumulated one query term at a time, needed when postings lists are not in a common order
ordering a postings list by a quantity such as tf rather than document ID
cluster the document vectors in preprocessing; at query time compute cosines only for documents in a few clusters
a generalization of champion lists: tier 1 holds postings with the highest tf, and query processing falls back to later tiers if fewer than K results
scoring that depends on omega, the width of the smallest window in a document that contains all the query terms
an aggregate scoring function that accumulates evidence of a document's relevance from multiple sources

code.snippet: FASTCOSINESCORE(q): float Scores[N]=0; for each d: Initialize Length[d]; for each query term t: calculate w_t,q and fetch postings list for t; for each pair (d, tf_t,d) in postings: add wf_t,d to Scores[d]; Read Length[d]; for each d: Scores[d] /= Length[d]; return Top K components of Scores[]
